title: Meta launches plan for $95B stock offering to fund AI expansion
content:
Meta said Monday it is planning to raise a total of $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure and superintelligence.
The stock was down 1.6% in morning trading after the announcement. Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares, Meta said in a statement.
The tech giant will initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.
The news comes as hyperscalers pour record sums into the AI infrastructure build-out. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031, across compute, data centers and power.
Meta's planned investments will support "emerging AI opportunities" including its family of apps, its AI agent Muse and its data center business, the company said Monday.
It plans to balance funding for these investments through a mix of operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, partnerships and equity capital.
Meta racing to secure AI infrastructure
Meta is among the major hyperscalers that are increasingly tapping debt to fund the expensive infrastructure required for the AI boom.
Last week, Meta posted third-quarter results showing revenue jumped 26% year on year: $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. However, investors focused more on the tech company's negative free cash flow and its higher full-year capital expenditure forecast.
It now expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from $130 billion. That sent Meta's shares lower on Thursday.
Meta is building four "superclusters" with more than 1 gigawatt of capacity each and is on track to nearly double total infrastructure capacity in 2026 on a year-over-year basis, the company said.
The decision to raise more money "reflects the eye-watering levels of investment required to keep up in the AI arms race," Ben Wood, senior partner at CCS Insight, told CNBC.
"Meta offering more stock comes at a time when numerous companies, such as Google, SpaceX and soon, Anthropic, are going to the markets to raise funds."
Alphabet, Google's parent company, said it would look to raise $85 billion in June. SpaceX has closed a $40 billion debt financing to purchase graphics processing units. Anthropic is preparing for an initial public offering.
TikTok U.S. is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity over the coming years, CNBC reported Friday.

report.summary: Meta plans to raise $95 billion through stock offerings to fund AI infrastructure, superintelligence, and data-center expansion.
report.background: Meta's move comes as hyperscalers pour record capital into AI compute, data centers, and power. Goldman Sachs estimates AI-related capital spending could reach about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031. Meta recently reported 26% revenue growth but drew investor concern over negative free cash flow and a higher full-year capex forecast of $135 billion to $145 billion. It is building four superclusters with more than 1 gigawatt of capacity each and aims to nearly double total infrastructure capacity in 2026. The equity raise reflects an AI arms race in which even cash-rich platforms are tapping public markets and debt to secure chips, energy, and data-center capacity.
key_points: Meta plans to raise $95 billion in two stages: $35 billion through underwritten public equity offerings, then $60 billion through an at-the-market program. The stock fell 1.6% in morning trading. Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom expressed interest in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares, signaling chip-supplier alignment with Meta's build-out.

The raise follows third-quarter results that beat revenue expectations but showed negative free cash flow and a higher capex range of $135 billion to $145 billion. Investors focused on the spending burden rather than sales growth, sending shares lower. Meta is balancing funding across operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, partnerships, and equity.

Meta says the money will support emerging AI opportunities across its family of apps, its AI agent Muse, and its data-center business. Its four superclusters each exceed 1 gigawatt, and the company expects to nearly double total infrastructure capacity year over year in 2026. That scale requires massive GPU, networking, cooling, and power investments.

Meta is not alone in seeking fresh capital. Alphabet said it would look to raise $85 billion, SpaceX closed $40 billion in debt financing for GPUs, Anthropic is preparing an IPO, and TikTok U.S. is seeking multiple gigawatts of computing capacity. The wave shows AI competition increasingly depends on access to public markets and credit, not just model quality.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Meta's $95 billion raise reinforces that frontier AI is becoming a capital-markets business, favoring firms that can access equity, debt, and chip partnerships. Smaller labs may face higher funding hurdles or become acquisition targets. For developers, more compute could accelerate model training and agent products, but platform dependence may grow as a few hyperscalers control capacity and pricing. Open-source ecosystems could benefit if Meta continues releasing Llama-family models, yet the infrastructure gap remains wide. For regular users, expect more capable AI agents and features inside Meta apps, alongside concerns about costs, privacy, and the concentration of AI power in a handful of companies.
report.tools: To follow the infrastructure trend, watch Meta's Llama models and Muse agent, plus PyTorch, vLLM, Ray, Kubernetes, and Hugging Face for serving and scaling AI workloads. These open-source tools help developers experiment with model deployment, distributed compute, and inference optimization without building a hyperscale data center.
